title: Tools of Financial Statement Analysis: Comparative and Common-Size Statements
summary: Financial statement analysis breaks the figures in financial statements into meaningful relationships. This chapter covers its objectives, types and limitations, and two tools: comparative statements (change over time) and common-size statements (each item as a percentage of a base).

notes.heading: Meaning, objectives and users
notes.html:
Financial statement analysis is the systematic process of examining the items of financial statements to judge profitability, liquidity, solvency and efficiency.

  • Objectives: assess earning capacity, short-term and long-term solvency, managerial efficiency; compare within the firm (intra-firm) and with other firms (inter-firm); forecast and budget.
  • Users: management, investors and shareholders, lenders and creditors, employees, government and tax authorities.

notes.heading: Types and tools of analysis
notes.html:
BasisHorizontal (dynamic) analysisVertical (static) analysis
MeaningCompares the same item over two or more yearsStudies the relationship between items of the same year
ToolComparative statementsCommon-size statements
Also calledTime-series analysisCross-sectional analysis

Other bases: external (by outsiders using published data) and internal (by management with full access).

Tools: comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis, cash flow statement.

notes.heading: Comparative statements
notes.html:
Show figures of two or more periods side by side with the absolute change and the percentage change.

  • Absolute change = Current year figure − Previous year figure
  • Percentage change = Absolute change ÷ Previous year figure × 100

Interpretation: revenue rose by 20% while expenses rose by only 15%, so profit grew faster (27.5%), showing better cost control.

notes.heading: Common-size statements
notes.html:
Each item is expressed as a percentage of a common base:

  • Common-size Statement of Profit and Loss: base = Revenue from Operations (100%).
  • Common-size Balance Sheet: base = Total of Equity and Liabilities / Total Assets (100%).

notes.heading: Limitations and common mistakes
notes.html:
• Analysis is only as reliable as the financial statements: it inherits their limitations (historical cost, window dressing).
  • Ignores price-level changes and qualitative factors.
  • Different accounting policies make inter-firm comparison misleading.
  • A single year's analysis has limited use; trends matter.

Common mistakes: dividing the change by the current-year figure instead of the previous year's; using total income instead of revenue from operations as the base; forgetting to show a decrease in brackets; rounding percentages inconsistently.

questions.q: What is meant by horizontal analysis?
questions.answerHtml: Horizontal analysis compares the figures of the same item over two or more accounting periods to study the change, for example through comparative statements.

questions.q: State any three objectives of financial statement analysis.
questions.answerHtml:
• Assess profitability: to know the earning capacity and its trend.
  • Assess solvency: to judge the ability to pay short-term and long-term debts.
  • Make comparisons: intra-firm and inter-firm comparison to locate strengths and weaknesses.
